h: Democracy without the vote: when the street becomes the last court
dek: Anilkumar Payyappilly Vijayan, an English professor and poet from Kerala, argues that striking names off the voter rolls has kept the shell of democracy but drained the life out of it, and that is why the young are on the streets.
body: Anilkumar Payyappilly Vijayan, a poet who teaches English at a government college in Kerala, opens with a Malayali joke: a cream biscuit has cream in it, but a Tiger biscuit has no tiger. Today's democracy, he says, is much the same. Like coffee without caffeine, the elections, Parliament and rituals remain, but the right to vote is being taken out, and he names Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar as the man getting it done.

Citing a report in Janata Weekly, the writer says the most names cut from the rolls belonged to Muslims, Christians, Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities) and migrant workers, and women lost even more. Removing the names of the dead is one thing; making the living vanish on paper is another. The Supreme Court refused to hear cases about bypoll seats quickly, saying these were only bypolls. For the writer, every name cut is a constitutional question.

Then he does the sums. In the 2024 general election the NDA won about 43.6 per cent of the votes cast, and turnout was 66.10 per cent. That puts its share of all registered voters at about 29 per cent. The writer says calling this everyone's mandate is wrong, and cutting names makes the picture worse.

This, he says, explains why the young and the opposition have taken to the streets: when there is no room left for a voice inside institutions, the street becomes the place to speak. And it has had an effect. Under pressure the Commission told BLOs (booth level officers) to collect documents at people's homes, announced that left-out voters would be added back, agreed to give parties readable rolls, and declared a special summary revision in 17 states.

Finally he recalls Ambedkar's warning that even a good constitution can fail in incapable hands, and asks the young to build something new with compassion, friendship and non-violence. Election victories do not last, he says; what lasts is what someone stood up for.
nazar: This article reminds us that democracy is not just an election date; it is every citizen being counted. When the support of about 29 per cent of voters is passed off as the will of all, and crores of names vanish from the rolls on top of that, the young people on the streets are not anarchists. They are citizens asking for an account.

The most important part is the writer's list of the steps the Commission has taken back. An institution that until yesterday would admit nothing bent as soon as pressure came. Pressure from the street is not wasted.
sawal: If your name is not even on the roll, where is your democracy?
ref: Universal adult franchise (Article 326)
The provision of the Constitution that gives every citizen over 18 the right to vote. There is no condition of education, property or caste.
Sortition (selection by lot)
The method of ancient Athens, where many posts were filled by drawing lots rather than by vote. Aristotle thought it more democratic than election.

h: Seven pillars, all shaking: a change of government will not fill the cracks
dek: Retired IAS officer V. Ramani tests democracy's seven pillars one by one and says the crisis of 13 crore names being cut is a symptom of a larger illness that elections alone will not cure.
body: Retired IAS officer V. Ramani, a member of the Constitutional Conduct Group, begins with the hundred years since T.E. Lawrence's book Seven Pillars of Wisdom. India's democracy too, he says, has seven pillars: the legislature, the executive, political parties, the judiciary, independent institutions, the media and civil society. Today all seven are shaking.

In the legislature, the Aaya Ram Gaya Ram habit of switching sides that began in 1967 has grown into whole groups changing parties, and presiding officers have never ruled against a defector. The opposition's demand to impeach the Chief Election Commissioner is also put off. The executive avoided public consultation on the CAA, the farm laws and the SIR, dismisses dissent as urban Naxal or sedition, and senior officers have all but stopped recording objections to illegal orders.

The courts are slow in cases about liberty, and under laws like the UAPA and PMLA the process itself has become the punishment. Those accused in the Bhima Koregaon and Delhi riots cases waited years for bail, and Stan Swamy and G.N. Saibaba died after the hardships of prison. Among independent institutions, the deepest wound is to the Election Commission: 13 crore names were cut from the rolls in the SIR.

On the media, he recalls Advani's words after the Emergency, that when asked to bend it crawled, and adds that today a large part of it does not even need to be asked. In civil society, polarisation has broken families and friendships, Muslims are being made into outsiders and Christians are being harassed in the name of conversion.

Ramani's conclusion is that changing the government alone will not end this illness. He repeats Ambedkar's warning that hero worship leads to dictatorship. The real work is to restore the broken trust between citizen and state, citizen and institutions, and citizens among themselves, a trust that rests on the Preamble's justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
nazar: This article puts the movement on a larger map. Even if Gyanesh Kumar resigns, the structure will remain in which Speakers stay silent on defections, courts take years over bail and channels nod along with power. That is why the street's demand is bigger than one officer.

It is worth noting that this comes from a former bureaucrat who knows the system from the inside. His complaint that officers stay silent on illegal orders fits today's Election Commission most exactly.
sawal: If the pillars themselves are hollow, what will a new face change?
ref: Anti-defection law
The Tenth Schedule of the Constitution, added in 1985. The Speaker or Chairman decides on the membership of an MP or MLA who leaves their party.
Constitutional Conduct Group
A group of retired civil servants that issues open letters and statements on constitutional values and the working of government.

h: The affidavit did not clear the doubts, it deepened them
dek: Shravasti Dasgupta shows in six points that the Election Commission's affidavit in the Supreme Court sidesteps, rather than answers, the questions raised about the commissioners' objections, Form 6 and ECINet.
body: On 26 October the Election Commission told the Supreme Court in an affidavit that all three SIR orders were issued with the consent of all three commissioners. In this analysis for The Wire Hindi, Shravasti Dasgupta argues that the affidavit does not refute the Indian Express report that commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu recorded 14 objections in ten months. The Commission only says a newspaper report is not legal evidence. It does not deny the facts.

According to the writer, the affidavit does not explain why some decisions were taken without the knowledge of the two commissioners. On Form 6 things get more tangled. The Commission says the form was not changed, but admits that a declaration was added to its online page for OTP or e-sign. Earlier this same declaration was described as approved by the Supreme Court; now it is a separate document.

In West Bengal, Commission officers filed 16.1 lakh appeals against voters whom judicial officers had already found eligible. The affidavit says these cases were not brought to the Commission's notice, but does not say who gave permission. In Goa, the centrally run ECINet software stopped local officers from restoring names, and the Commission is silent on why names did not come back even after eight applications in seven days.

According to file notings, the IT department built modules without telling the Commission, and the commissioners learnt of it from the media. Joshi had recommended a committee of outside experts. A committee of experts from IIT Bombay and IISc Bengaluru has now been formed, but the affidavit does not even mention the earlier concerns.

The last point concerns the commissioners' letters to Cabinet Secretary T.V. Somanathan, which complained of an order on the division of work issued by Deputy Election Commissioner Manish Garg without consultation. The affidavit brushes this off as a misunderstanding.
nazar: The affidavit was given to the court, but its real reader is the voter whose name was cut. For that voter, being told that a newspaper report is not evidence is no answer. It is a defensive trick.

When two of the Commission's own commissioners have recorded written objections, the claim of consensus will stand only if the files are opened. The Supreme Court should call for the file notings itself.
sawal: If there was consensus, why the fear of showing the files?
ref: ECINet
The Election Commission's centrally run digital platform, which holds the full database of voter rolls. It is alleged that it tied the hands of officers on the ground.
Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu
The Commission's two other commissioners, alongside Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The report of their recorded objections brought differences within the Commission into the open.
photo_note: Representative image: London's Old Bailey court, historical illustration.

h: Take down the photo, the idea stays: Raihan Vadra's exhibition and the fear of power
dek: Frontline's political editor Anand Mishra places the removal of 75 photographs of July's Gen Z protest from Bikaner House within a long history of curbs on art and books, and asks whether an idea can be erased by taking it off a wall.
body: In his newsletter, Frontline's political editor Anand Mishra takes up the row that set social media boiling. At Delhi's Bikaner House, 75 of the 105 photographs in 26-year-old Raihan Rajiv Vadra's exhibition No Idea Is Final were taken down. The photographs were of July's Gen Z protest. The venue, run under the Rajasthan government, said the pictures went against its guidelines.

Raihan said art recognises no political borders, and his mother Priyanka Gandhi Vadra commented on the fear of the powerful. BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia called it a matter not of expression but of a political launch. The writer asks whether, by calling it a launch, the BJP is not shooting itself in the foot. The very next day Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan offered to host the whole exhibition in his state.

Mishra then recalls older cases. In 2018 two pictures featuring Jinnah were removed from a Gandhi Jayanti exhibition at Aligarh Muslim University and the librarian was served a notice. In 2002 a photograph of two men kissing was taken down under pressure at Mumbai's Jehangir Art Gallery. The Bajrang Dal attacked M.F. Husain's home in 1998; he left the country in 2006 and died in London in 2011.

The story of books is the same. Bengal's BJP government forcibly removed Left parties' bookstalls set up outside puja pandals. The Nehru government had seized Nathuram Godse's court statement, but the writer points out that no such ban stopped the rise of the right. In 2014, in the Aveek Sarkar case, the Supreme Court said a work must be judged in its full context.
The writer's question is simply this: does removing a photograph or a bookstall also remove the idea? The answer lies in the very examples he lists.
nazar: When a movement being stopped on the street cannot find room for its pictures even on a gallery wall, that is a sign not of rules but of fear. The sit-in was removed from Jantar Mantar; now the photographs from the wall.
The irony is that the removed photographs will now reach more people than before. When power starts to fear the camera, it tells us itself how much truth there is in the picture from the street.
sawal: Does a photo taken off the wall also leave our memory?
ref: Bikaner House
An old Rajasthan government building near India Gate in Delhi, now a venue for art exhibitions and cultural events.
Aveek Sarkar vs State of West Bengal (2014)
In this judgment the Supreme Court dropped the British-era Hicklin test for obscenity and adopted a community standards test, under which a work is seen in its full context.

h: Drunk on power: face down in the gutter, sure they are standing tall
dek: In Vishnu Nagar's satire, twelve years of power have gone to the head so badly that even the anger of young people on the streets looks like a passing wave.
body: Vishnu Nagar's satire opens with a picture. Someone dead drunk lies face down in a filthy drain, thinking he is standing with his chest puffed out. Everyone can see the state he is in, except him. The pointer is at the ruling camp.

This character in the drain does not keep quiet either. He gives speeches, shouts, issues orders, hurls abuse and sings songs of his own bravery. At the mere mention of a change of government he panics and starts calling his opponent mad. According to the writer, more than twelve years of power, which in his view survived on lies and dishonesty, has now become an intoxication, and this intoxication does not wear off for a long time even after power is gone.

He also pokes fun at claims of standing. Even in Ayodhya, where the temple was built, the cheering that is so loudly advertised no longer rings out. Demands to remove Dharmendra Pradhan and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar kept looking trivial to this character, and he is sure this wave of protest will settle by itself.

But the real target of the satire is the fear that is now changing. According to the writer, young men and women are on the streets despite police lathis, tear gas, detentions and shutdowns of the internet and the metro, and what scares the regime most is that its fear is leaving people's minds. He also recalls the question raised in court about who decided to remove Jantar Mantar from the list of protest sites, and the voter roll errors the government is now having to admit.

In the end the writer says this frightened power keeps going back to its comfortable air-conditioned room. Those who live in illusions should be left to themselves; one day they will come down to earth on their own.
nazar: The strength of satire is that it stings more than a slogan. Vishnu Nagar catches the arrogance that treats every demand as trivial and every movement as a wave.
There is a lesson in it for the movement too: waiting for power to come down to earth on its own is not enough. To bring it down to earth, you have to stay on the street.
sawal: If fear is gone, what will power stand on?
ref: Vishnu Nagar
A senior Hindi poet, satirist and journalist. His satire column appears every week in Navjivan.
Jantar Mantar
The spot near Parliament in Delhi that for years has been set aside for sit-ins and protests. In this movement the question of the ban on protests there reached the court.
photo_note: Bengal's rising son-in-law, a caricature by Gaganendranath Tagore

h: The 1 November rally: the hurdles are ready, and so is the resolve
dek: An Urdu editorial in Siasat says attempts to stop and dampen the Ramlila Maidan rally have already begun, so the INDIA alliance must stay alert until the last day.
body: This editorial in Siasat, the Urdu newspaper from Hyderabad, opens with a couplet meaning that every night is followed by a morning. The subject is the INDIA alliance rally, led by the Congress, against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on 1 November. The organisers hope about ten lakh people will come from across the country; workers in many states are mobilising people and convoys will set out from some states.

According to the paper, the hurdles are already visible. The Congress alleges that the special trains it asked for have not been arranged. The police gave permission, but with conditions, and the party says new conditions keep being imposed on it. In the editorial's view, the government has already damaged the democratic process and now wants to silence those who have come out to save it.

The editorial alleges that the BJP pushed Delhi's traders forward, and they asked Rahul Gandhi to put off the rally, citing their business. Rahul Gandhi replied that if the Prime Minister removes Gyanesh Kumar, the movement will end in thirty seconds. According to the paper, the aim of such moves is to postpone the rally, stall preparations, cool the workers' enthusiasm and then call the rally a failure. So far these attempts have not succeeded.

The paper is confident the rally will be historic, that people will be able to express their anger over the SIR irregularities openly, and that the campaign against Gyanesh Kumar will gain new strength. It says the government and the BJP also understand that the rally will increase pressure on them, which is why the tactics to stop it will continue until the day of the rally. So the Congress and the alliance parties should stay alert, give no one a chance to spoil the atmosphere and bow to no obstacle.
nazar: The right to peaceful assembly is not a convenience granted to a party; it is every citizen's right. Trains not being provided, or conditions piled on conditions, may seem small, but they decide whether a man from a distant village can reach Delhi with what he has to say.
The rally's success will not be measured by the size of the crowd, but by how loudly the voice of voters whose names were cut is heard.
sawal: What fear does the attempt to stop a rally reveal?
ref: Ramlila Maidan
A large ground in Delhi where the 2011 Anna movement also took place. It is a long-standing venue for big political rallies.
INDIA alliance
An alliance of opposition parties including the Congress, formed in 2023. It is now running a campaign to remove Gyanesh Kumar.

h: A Commission that taunts: why has a constitutional body's tongue gone sour?
dek: Samiratmaj Mishra asks why, while answering a voter roll mistake, the office of Uttar Pradesh's Chief Electoral Officer chose taunts over facts, and what that does to the Commission's credibility.
body: This DW Hindi article, published on Webdunia, moves from a small mistake to a big question. In the voter roll for the graduates' constituency of the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council, the name Ramhit Yadav was printed in such a way that it read as 'Ram killed Yadav'. The office explained that the software had translated, word for word, a name entered in English.

Aam Aadmi Party Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Singh asked whether computers too discriminate by caste. In reply, the office's official handle wrote a sarcastic post saying software is not casteist, and took a dig at communalism too. After anger from the opposition and on social media, the office apologised on 27 October and admitted that such language did not befit an official handle.

Senior journalist Amita Verma says a senior officer like Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa is expected to show restraint, not to reply like a political opponent. According to Professor Satish Prakash of Meerut, there is a difference between facts, legal clarification and political taunts, and an institution's credibility is also built by its language. The writer asks who wrote the post and who approved it.

This tone is not a one-off. The article recalls that in August 2025 Gyanesh Kumar asked Rahul Gandhi to file an affidavit or apologise, and in April 2026 a Trinamool delegation accused him of rude behaviour. In Pilibhit, errors were found in all 10,470 approved Form 8 entries, in Azamgarh several entries with identical names were found, and a review was ordered across the state.

According to journalist Sanjay Kumar, the movement of the young and the parties has forced the Commission to listen, admit mistakes and correct them, and reports of differences within the Commission have put it on the defensive.
nazar: An institution that keeps account of the votes of crores of people owes humility first of all. Taunting over a mistake shows that the Commission has begun to see itself not as accountable but as a party to the fight.
The apology is welcome, but the Pilibhit and Azamgarh figures show the problem runs deeper than language. Let the tongue be mended, and the rolls with it.
sawal: Why should the office that counts our votes speak in taunts?
ref: Chief Electoral Officer
The Election Commission's top officer in each state, who oversees the voter roll and election arrangements. The officer answers directly to the Commission.
Form 8
The form filled to correct details in the voter roll or change an address. In Pilibhit, irregularities are alleged through this form.

h: Israel's election: Netanyahu not beaten, Arab votes hold the balance
dek: After a record turnout no camp has reached a majority, and the key to the outcome lies with the Arab parties that both sides kept at arm's length.
body: On 27 October Israel recorded a turnout of 77.7 per cent, the highest since 1999. By Wednesday afternoon, with about 80 per cent counted, Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc looked set for 54 seats, while a majority in the 120-seat parliament needs 61. Gadi Eisenkot's opposition was at 49. The Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List hold the balance with 17 seats.

According to this Al Jazeera analysis, the biggest story is the turnout of Palestinian citizens. In this community, a fifth of the population, some estimates put turnout as high as 80 per cent. Experts see it as a response to the government's harsh treatment after 7 October 2023.

But the article shows that anti-Arab rhetoric was not confined to one camp. Likud made baseless claims that the opposition would form a government with the help of Arab parties, and even petitioned to bar the Joint List. On the other side, Lieberman ruled out an alliance with Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties, and Bennett said there was no mandate to govern with Arab parties after 7 October, even though Ra'am was part of his own government in 2021-22.

The road ahead is tangled. Whoever President Herzog judges most capable will get 28 days, and 14 more if needed. Analyst Daniel Levy lists four possibilities: another election, defections from the opposition, a unity government led by Netanyahu, or an Eisenkot minority government with Arab support, which he thinks the least likely. New military tension with Iran could also become an excuse for an emergency government.

Eisenkot's campaign rested on ending the army exemption for ultra-Orthodox youth and an independent inquiry into the security failure of 7 October. In psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal's view, most Israelis want change but are not ready to go along with Arab parties, and that is the real knot of the moment.
nazar: The lesson of this election is that a minority pushed to the margins again and again by power can register its presence through the vote, yet majoritarian politics is still not ready to treat it as a partner. When the opposition too avoids it, a wide gap remains between changing the government and changing policy.
In India too, the habit of seeing the minority vote as a 'burden' is old. Israel's deadlock shows that democracy is incomplete until every citizen's vote carries equal weight.
sawal: What if a minority's vote is counted but the minority is never taken along?
ref: Ra'am and the Joint List
The two main political fronts of Israel's Palestinian citizens. Ra'am (Mansour Abbas) in 2021 became the first to join an Israeli coalition government.
Haredi army exemption
The exemption from compulsory military service long given to ultra-Orthodox Jewish (Haredi) youth, which has been a source of conflict in Israeli politics for years.

h: From Yemen's mountains, a view of American power in decline
dek: Juan Cole argues that after the failure of the Iran war the Houthis are getting the better of Saudi Arabia, while America stands by and watches.
body: Historian Juan Cole's article, from TomDispatch, appeared in The Intercept. His argument is that the Iran war that began in February 2026 has turned out to be America's biggest retreat in the region since it left Vietnam in 1975, and that Yemen's Ansarullah, the Houthis, is now taking advantage of that weakness.

According to the writer, Iranian strikes destroyed or damaged hundreds of buildings and dozens of aircraft at American bases in eight countries. The naval base in Bahrain and the air command centre at Al-Udeid in Qatar were put out of action, and troops pulled back from Iraq. Cheap drones costing up to twenty thousand dollars emptied stocks of interceptor missiles costing four million dollars each.

Meanwhile, the ceasefire in Yemen that had held since 2022 broke. In July Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa airport to stop a Houthi delegation returning from Khamenei's funeral. In response the Houthis adopted a policy of 'blockade for blockade': three months of attacks on Saudi refineries, Aramco sites and airports, the closure of Riyadh's international airport in October, and the capture of Mokha port above the Bab al-Mandab.

Cole thinks the 'Iran-backed militia' label is wrong. In his account Ansarullah rules about 80 per cent of Yemen's population, its roots lie in the Zaydi tradition and Arab nationalism, and Iran's help is small next to the weapons America sold Saudi Arabia. Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt promised to defend Saudi Arabia, but none is keen to go into Yemen, and America has refused to intervene.

The writer sees it as like Vietnam: part of a bigger war, but really a fight for autonomy between poor mountain people and rich sheikhs. His conclusion is that this war will not decide the US-Iran contest, but it does bear witness to the decline of American power.
nazar: Every war in the Gulf reaches India's doorstep: through the price of oil, the safety of the lakhs of Indians who work there, and the trade that moves along the Red Sea route. Cole's analysis reminds us that claiming 'victory' in war is easy; its price is paid far and long.
This article is a forceful reading from one side, but its core question is fair: when even a superpower shrinks from protecting its ally, on whom can the region rest its trust in security?
sawal: How long can costly power hold out against cheap drones?
ref: Ansarullah (Houthis)
A Zaydi Shia movement of northern Yemen that took over Sanaa in 2015. That same year a Saudi-led coalition began bombing Yemen.
Bab al-Mandab
The narrow sea passage linking the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. A large share of Asia-Europe trade passes through it.

h: A Pakistan for all, or for a handful?
dek: Niaz Murtaza writes that a politics of wiping out opponents is increasing the state's power but eating away its credibility.
body: Political economist Niaz Murtaza starts with a simple framework. Countries emerging from colonial rule needed four pillars: a capable state, a working economy, a united nation and a politics that takes everyone along. In societies marked by diversity and inequality the last two were the most important, yet most governments neglected exactly these. Pakistan, the writer says, is on the same road.

He charges that Pakistan's politics runs on the principle of 'winner takes all'. Over the past four years the PTI and nationalist parties in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and, recently, Azad Kashmir have not merely been defeated through judicial, electoral and administrative steps; there has been an attempt to finish them off. Emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is the latest link in this chain. The writer says many experts at home and abroad regard the 2024 election as openly rigged.

The separation of powers has broken down too. The lines between the executive, parliament and the judiciary have blurred so much that the three look like a troika. Lower down, most provinces have not held local elections for years, the provinces have grabbed the powers of local bodies, and the centre is weakening the provinces.

On civil liberties, the writer cites the latest annual report of the Human Rights Commission (HRCP). Journalists, political workers, lawyers and activists face weak cases under cybercrime, sedition and terrorism laws, and fear of threats and enforced disappearance has made speaking out risky.

The conclusion is sharp: a Pakistan for all has become a Pakistan for a handful. The rulers are gaining power but losing trust, and force is taking the place of consent. Without inclusive politics, the writer says, a strong nation, a capable state and progress are all castles in the air.
nazar: Murtaza's framework is not about Pakistan alone. Wherever an opposition party starts being treated as an enemy rather than a rival, local elections keep getting postponed and the powers of provinces slide towards the centre, the structure of democracy stays standing but grows hollow inside.

Indian readers should not move on thinking this is a neighbour's story. This gap between power and credibility is a question for every country where those in power have begun to see dissent as a threat.
sawal: When power grows and trust shrinks, how long can a rule last?
ref: HRCP
The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, an independent civil body working since 1987, which publishes a yearly report on the state of human rights in the country.
PTI
Imran Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf. Since being removed from power in 2022, the party and its leaders have faced constant cases and restrictions.

h: Sahil Wakode: batons for mourners, trolls for questions
dek: Vikrant Kishore writes that the death of a Dalit student at IIT Bombay must be investigated on evidence, not on the verdict of a mob.
body: On 25 October, police detained at least 20 of the people who had come to Mumbai's Chaityabhoomi to light candles in memory of Sahil Wakode and demand an inquiry, reportedly including Sahil's parents. Women are alleged to have been pushed around. The police called the gathering unauthorised. The writer, Vikrant Kishore, who teaches at the University of Nottingham Ningbo China, sees this as a disturbing pattern.

The facts are these: on 18 September Sahil died by suicide in his hostel. IIT Bombay first said he had cheated in an exam using a phone and ChatGPT, then three days later withdrew the statement and apologised. The family alleges caste harassment and a threat of suspension. An FIR for abetment of suicide and under the SC/ST Act has been filed against a professor, who denies the allegations. The institute denies discrimination.

The writer stresses that support or rhetoric cannot decide the allegations. The inquiry must look at what happened in the exam hall, whether Sahil was made to write an apology, and whether he was allowed to finish the paper, as the 2015 rules required. He also recalls figures placed in Parliament: from 2020-21 to 2024-25, 45 students took their lives across 23 IITs, of whom 28 were SC, ST or OBC, though this does not prove that caste caused every death.

A large part of the article deals with the 'victim card' taunt. According to the writer, this taunt paints a complaint about equality as a ploy and turns attention to the motives of the person complaining. On social media Sahil's parents were called 'greedy' and 'liars' and the protest was called 'drama'.

The writer's demand is clear: begin the inquiry with evidence, CCTV, messages and witnesses; let the police answer for the detentions and the use of force; and let Sahil, his family and fellow students have the right to due process, just as the professor does.
nazar: The strength of this article is its restraint. It blames no one, it only asks for an equal process. But that very demand weighs most heavily on institutions that first accuse a student and later apologise, and on police who turn a condolence meeting into a law and order problem.

In our view, the real question is the language of 'merit' that puts a Dalit student in the dock of suspicion at every step. Until campuses have a trustworthy route for complaints and discipline without humiliation, such deaths will go on becoming statistics.
sawal: Does a student who has died have no right to due process?
ref: Chaityabhoomi
Dr Ambedkar's memorial in Dadar, Mumbai. Every year on 6 December lakhs of people come here to pay tribute.
SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
A 1989 law that sets special punishments and procedures for caste crimes against Dalits and Adivasis.

h: Addis Ababa: the war was not 'at the door', it had been inside the house for years
dek: As the Tigray war reaches the capital, Rachel Dubale asks what we turned our eyes away from after the peace deal.
body: Rachel Dubale is a fellow at the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Her essay opens with a childhood memory: her father would put his palm over her eyes to 'make' darkness, and the fear would vanish. As an adult she kept doing the same, only instead of a palm there were pleasant pictures.

In 2022 she came to Addis Ababa to learn the Ge'ez script. By then the Tigray war, fought mainly between Tigrayan forces led by the TPLF and the federal government, was two years old. The Pretoria agreement came in November 2022, but the war's effects kept showing up in fragments in the capital.

She lists those fragments. In January 2023, at the Timkat festival, police stopped her for wearing traditional dress from the Amhara region, because the cloth was seen as a political statement of Amhara identity. In March the celebration of the Adwa victory was divided too: pictures of Menelik and Taytu, even a flag without an emblem, became disputes, and shops printing and selling them were reportedly shut down.

Still, she admits, her own daily life did not change much, while within the same borders people were being killed and uprooted. Four years later she is in Addis again. Fighting has broken out again between federal and Tigrayan forces, old enemies have formed an 'Alliance for Survival' against the government, hospitals in the northwest are full of patients, and the evenings bring checkpoints, rumours and unconfirmed reports of blasts near the military headquarters.

The writer argues that after Pretoria many mistook the absence of open war for peace, while land disputes, the question of disarmament, mistrust and ethnic rifts remained. Newspapers write 'war at the door', but she asks whose door it is. Now, she says, we must keep our eyes open, even if the rest of the world looks away.
nazar: This essay reminds us that people in capitals think of a war as 'far away' until the blasts reach their own street. From Manipur to Kashmir, India too knows that paper agreements and claims that 'things are normal' do not heal the cracks on the ground.
News from Ethiopia rarely finds space in Indian papers. Dubale's point applies to us too: whoever looks away from the suffering of others is also slow to recognise the fire in their own home.
sawal: Is the absence of open war really peace?
ref: Pretoria agreement
The ceasefire signed in November 2022 between the Ethiopian government and the TPLF, which formally halted the two-year Tigray war.
Battle of Adwa
In 1896 the army of Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu defeated Italy. It is a great symbol of victory against colonialism in Africa.

h: 'Buy only from Hindus': not self-reliance but a call to boycott
dek: An analysis in Sabrang India says minister Nitesh Rane's call is meant to push Muslims out of their livelihoods and to frighten them.
body: Maharashtra minister and BJP leader Nitesh Rane was speaking at the launch of HARHAR, a new Hindu organisation of hotel and restaurant owners, in Jui Nagar, Navi Mumbai. According to Sabrang India, in a video on his official X handle he says Hindus should buy only from Hindus, and links this to strengthening a Hindu Rashtra (Hindu nation).

Rane did not stop there. He demanded that Muslims not be allowed to set up shops at the coming Nashik Simhastha Kumbh, and, according to the article, even threatened that Muslims who go there should not return safe and sound. Using phrases like 'love jihad', 'land jihad' and 'halal jihad', he claimed that Muslim traders' money is used against Hindus. The article notes that no solid evidence for this was offered there.

The article accepts that organising traders and promoting local products and food traditions are fair goals. But it asks why helping Hindu business should rest on boycotting Muslims. Real self-reliance comes from local production, small enterprises, supply chains and jobs, and a religious boycott does none of these.

The analysis says such calls turn everyday buying and selling into a communal decision, where a shopkeeper's religion alone becomes a reason for suspicion. At an event like the Kumbh there can be rules for licences, cleanliness and safety, but a blanket ban based on religion raises questions about equality and the right to earn a living.

The article recalls Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution and says a threat of violence from the mouth of a serving minister is especially serious. Its conclusion is that no citizen should fear losing their livelihood or their life because of their religion.
nazar: The market has always been the place where different people learn to trust one another. When a minister himself calls for breaking that trust, the loss is not only the Muslim shopkeeper's but that of the shared life on which towns and cities run.
In our view, the real question is accountability. If a minister who has sworn an oath to the Constitution makes open threats and nothing happens, that silence too becomes a message.
sawal: Whom do goods bought after asking the shopkeeper's religion really strengthen?
ref: Simhastha Kumbh, Nashik
The Kumbh Mela held every twelve years on the banks of the Godavari at Nashik-Trimbakeshwar, drawing lakhs of pilgrims and thousands of shopkeepers.
Article 15
The provision of the Constitution that bars discrimination on grounds of religion, caste, sex or place of birth, including access to shops and public places.
photo_note: A craftsman making baskets and fans, representative image

h: A rape case cannot be ended by 'compromise': Supreme Court
dek: The survivor told the court she had been pressured into a compromise; the Supreme Court set aside the High Court order and directed that the trial go ahead.
body: The Supreme Court made clear on Wednesday that a case of a serious crime like rape cannot be ended simply because the survivor and the accused have reached a compromise. A bench of Justice J.B. Pardiwala and Justice K. Vinod Chandran was hearing Gopal Lodhi vs State of Madhya Pradesh. The accused faces rape-related sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita along with sections of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.

The Madhya Pradesh High Court, using its inherent powers, had accepted the compromise and closed the case. The Supreme Court said it was troubled by this. Citing earlier judgments, the bench pointed out that heinous crimes are not private disputes, and that quashing, on the basis of a compromise alone, a crime the law does not allow to be compromised is beyond the court's jurisdiction.

The most important point came from the survivor's statement. The court spoke to her at the office of the District Legal Services Authority, in the presence of its secretary. She said she had been pressured into the compromise, that she was not willing, and that she needed money. She said her complaint was true. The court voiced concern about compromises made under pressure, as well as about false complaints made in the hope of money.

The bench set aside the High Court order and directed that the trial proceed. The accused was granted anticipatory bail with conditions. The court said whether the charges are true will be decided at trial.
nazar: In cases involving Dalit and poor women, 'compromise' is often another name for pressure, threats and helplessness. In this case too the survivor herself said she was not willing. The court did right to hear her voice directly rather than trust a compromise written on paper. The lower courts should follow the same approach.
sawal: Is a compromise made out of helplessness really a compromise?
ref: Section 528 BNSS
The section that replaced Section 482 of the old CrPC, giving High Courts the inherent power to quash cases in the interest of justice.
Compoundable offences
Offences in which the law lets the victim and the accused end the case by mutual settlement; rape is not one of them.

h: Jamia: they went to deliver water and got three days in judicial custody
dek: The sit-in for restoring the students' union reached its 17th day, Section 163 was imposed outside the campus, and three young men were sent to jail as a preventive measure.
body: At Jamia Millia Islamia the sit-in demanding restoration of the students' union (JMISU) reached its 17th day on Wednesday, and five students are on hunger strike. Union elections have not been held here since 2005. Classes are running online, Section 163 of the BNSS was imposed in the area on Tuesday, and Delhi Police and central forces are posted at every gate. Students standing outside say even food and water are not being allowed in.

On Monday evening police detained three young men near the gate: Niranjan K.S. of AIRSO, Munna Qureshi, a student doing a yoga course, and Arbaz Mewati, a former Jamia student. On Tuesday a special executive magistrate sent all three to three days in judicial custody under 'kalandra' proceedings. Mewati says he was trying to give water to the students sitting inside. The police daily diary records charges of gathering a crowd and forcing their way in.
According to defence lawyer M.B. Javed Iqbal, the court did not record his arguments and an important prosecution document was not given to him, which goes against natural justice.

The administration has said elections will be held 15 days after the union's constitution is approved, but has given no date. The students want the constitution by 20 December and elections by 6 February. Several students face campus bans and notices, and some have been asked to leave the hostel. The administration and police did not reply to Newslaundry's questions.
nazar: A university that has held no elections for twenty years is now blocking water to those who ask for elections, and the police are sending young people to jail in the name of prevention. A students' union is the first school of democracy. The Jamia administration should give a date, not lock the gates.
sawal: Why did the campus gates close on a demand for elections?
ref: Kalandra
A preventive police action in which a person is brought before a magistrate not for a criminal offence but over a feared breach of the peace.
Section 163 BNSS
The section that replaced the old Section 144, under which the administration can ban gatherings in an area.

h: Rewa nuclear plant: the gram sabha said 'no', so why an NOC?
dek: After the death of Adivasi woman Vimla Kol during a jal satyagraha, the conflict over the proposed nuclear project in Rewa has deepened.
body: A nuclear power project is proposed near the villages of Rojhauhi and Sarai Kala in the Sirmaur area of Rewa district, Madhya Pradesh. It is still at an early stage, and the dispute is over drilling and technical tests. According to the report, even basic information has not been made public: the reactor's capacity, how much land is needed, which villages will be affected and how much water it will use.

Leader of the Opposition Umang Singhar alleges that on 3 September the gram sabha (village assembly) unanimously refused permission for drilling, and the panchayat informed the administration in writing on 5 September. Despite this, on 23 September an NOC was issued on the basis of an alleged consent letter dated 4 September. On 8 October sarpanch Komal Sanjay Singh asked the Commissioner and the Collector to investigate this letter and cancel the NOC.

Meanwhile Vimla Kol, an Adivasi woman from Rojhauhi who had been on a jal satyagraha (water protest) with the villagers for about four days, fell ill on the night of 21 October and died in hospital on 22 October. According to Singhar, more than 1,500 families live in the two villages, among them Adivasis, Dalits, small farmers and farm labourers.

Singhar has demanded that studies on the environment, earthquake risk, water and radiation be made public. According to the report, the government and the administration have not yet responded to the allegations about the consent letter.
nazar: Even in the age of PESA and the Forest Rights Act, if a gram sabha's 'no' can be turned into a 'yes' by a doubtful letter, what does consent even mean in Adivasi areas? An account of Vimla Kol's death and an independent inquiry into the consent letter are both necessary. For a project like a nuclear plant, transparency should be the first condition.
sawal: Who turned the gram sabha's 'no' into a 'yes' on paper?
ref: Jal satyagraha
A peaceful protest carried out by standing or sitting in water, made famous in Madhya Pradesh by the movements of people displaced by dams.
NOC
No Objection Certificate, a written approval from a local body or department saying it has no objection to a piece of work.

h: Damoh: two Muslims taking buffaloes beaten, no case filed
dek: A mob stripped the cattle traders and beat them with bats, they were laid on the floor in hospital, and the police say no complaint has come in.
body: There are reports of a mob attack on two Muslim cattle traders, Abid Qureshi and Hasan Qureshi, in Madhya Pradesh's Damoh district. According to the report, they were taking buffaloes with their companion Hussain Khan towards a gaushala (cow shelter) in Sagar when a group stopped them. When they tried to get away, bricks were thrown at them and they had to stop.

It is alleged that the two were then stripped, tied with ropes and beaten with sticks and bats. The attackers accused them of cattle theft and cow slaughter, while the two kept begging for mercy. The report holds Bajrang Dal workers responsible for the attack. Hussain Khan somehow escaped.

The two badly injured traders were taken to a nearby hospital, where they were laid on the floor. Videos of both the beating and the hospital are circulating on social media. The injured have named Deepak Nema, Chhutka and Nikhil Chaurasia. The report makes clear that these allegations have not been independently verified.

According to the police, no case had been registered at the time of writing because no one came forward to complain. Officials are currently checking the papers for the purchase and transport of the buffaloes.
nazar: The video exists, the injured are in hospital, the names are out, and yet the police wait for a complaint while the inquiry is into the victims' papers. In cases of serious violence the police can register a case themselves. The Supreme Court's guidelines on mob violence were meant for exactly such moments.
sawal: With the video right there, why wait for a complaint?
ref: Tehseen Poonawalla judgment
In 2018 the Supreme Court issued directions to prevent mob violence, such as a nodal officer in every district, immediate FIRs and fast-track trials.

h: Siang dam: arrests over protests, hunger strike in custody
dek: After the violence in Pasighat at least 26 people, including five minors, have been arrested, and a leader of the movement is fasting in custody.
body: The movement against the proposed mega dam on the Siang river in Arunachal Pradesh has taken a sharp turn. At least 26 people, including five minors, have been arrested in connection with the violence in Pasighat, East Siang, on 23 October. That day, organisations opposing the project had called a 12-hour bandh (shutdown).

Lawyer and activist Ebo Mili and youth leader Otul Jerang surrendered at Pasighat police station on 24 October. Mili is on hunger strike even in police custody. Jerang has existing illnesses and depends on medicines; he broke his fast when his health worsened. According to district SP Pankaj Lamba, eight cases have been registered over the events of 23 October and six people have been held for questioning.

The protesters' demands are: that work on the pre-feasibility report stop at once, that those detained be freed, that the FIRs be cancelled and that the central armed forces deployed for the project be withdrawn.

The government describes the 11,200 megawatt Siang Upper Multipurpose Project as an answer to China's 60,000 megawatt Medog dam and a means of water security. NITI Aayog proposed it in 2017. People in more than 27 villages along the Siang have opposed it for years, fearing the drowning of ancestral land, displacement and damage to the ecology of this earthquake-prone region.
nazar: Instead of talking to those whose land will be drowned, the government has filled the villages with paramilitary forces. The violence must be investigated, but treating the whole movement as a crime will break the trust without which no project can last in a border region. Competition with China should not come at the cost of the Adivasi communities who live there.
sawal: In the name of national security, who will ask the villages for their consent?
ref: Siang river
The river called the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, which becomes the Siang in Arunachal and the main stream of the Brahmaputra in Assam.
Pre-feasibility report
The early technical, geological and hydrological study done before a big project, for which drilling and surveys are carried out.

h: Workers left out of the new definition of 'industry': AITUC moves the Supreme Court
dek: The trade union has challenged Section 2(p) of the Industrial Relations Code, which keeps charitable institutions and 'sovereign functions' out of the definition of industry.
body: The Tamil Nadu unit of the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) has filed a petition in the Supreme Court challenging Section 2(p) of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020. This section decides what an 'industry' is. The petition questions three kinds of exclusions from this definition: institutions doing charitable, social or philanthropic service, activities linked to the government's 'sovereign functions', and any work the central government leaves out by notification.

The Code was made in September 2020 and came into force on 21 November 2025, ending the Industrial Disputes Act of 1947. The petition rests on the 20 August judgment of a nine-judge Constitution bench, which kept the Bangalore Water Supply test for old cases but left open the question of whether Section 2(p) is valid.

The union argues that these exclusions are based not on the nature of the work but on the identity of the employer, which runs against the 'triple test' and violates Articles 14, 19(1)(c) and 21 of the Constitution. Welfare or public service work does not become a sovereign function just because the government does it. And no test or procedure has been laid down for the open-ended power given to the centre to leave things out.

On Wednesday, before the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan said the Constitution bench had deliberately left this issue open. The Chief Justice said he would look into it. The report records no formal order.
nazar: Once the definition of industry is narrowed, lakhs of people working in hospitals, trusts and government schemes can lose the right to raise disputes, challenge retrenchment and bargain through a union. The Bangalore Water Supply judgment shut this road half a century ago. The court must see whether the new Code is reopening it through the back door.
sawal: If the employer is a charity, do the worker's rights shrink?
ref: Bangalore Water Supply judgment
A 1978 Supreme Court judgment that laid down the 'triple test': systematic activity, cooperation between employer and workers, and the production of goods or services people need.
Industrial Relations Code
One of the four new labour codes, which replaced three old laws on trade unions, industrial disputes and standing orders.

h: Drought in 18 districts of Gujarat and Rajasthan, Rs 8,500 a hectare for farmers
dek: After a weak monsoon, 14 districts in Rajasthan and four in Gujarat have been declared drought-hit, and nearly half the country's land is in the grip of drought.
body: The toll of this year's weak monsoon is now being entered in government records. Rajasthan has declared 14 of its 41 districts drought-hit, and Gujarat four districts. Across the two states, crops have failed in 18 districts and farmers are in distress.

According to Met department figures, Rajasthan received 340.2 millimetres of rain between 1 June and 30 September, against a normal average of 435.6 millimetres for the period. That is a shortfall of 22 per cent. The drought-hit districts include western ones like Churu, Jaisalmer, Jalore, Pali, Jodhpur, Bikaner, Barmer and Balotra, where farming and livestock rearing already depend on the rain.

In Gujarat, Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel announced relief in Gandhinagar on 26 October for farmers in Devbhumi Dwarka, Porbandar, Jamnagar and Kutch. He said the state as a whole received about 89 per cent of normal rain, but these four districts got less than the rest. The decision was taken under the centre's 2016 drought manual.

The relief package includes compensation of Rs 8,500 per hectare for crop loss under State Disaster Response Fund rules, up to a maximum of two hectares per farmer. Fodder will be sold at a subsidised rate of two rupees a kilo, gaushalas (cow shelters) will get 80 rupees for each animal, and from 1 November the affected districts are promised 150 days of work under the new rural employment scheme VB-G RAM G.

The crisis is not limited to these two states. Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh have already declared drought in parts of their territory, Maharashtra in as many as 265 talukas. According to IIT Gandhinagar's India Drought Monitor, 46.7 per cent of the country's land was in drought as of 21 October.
nazar: Declaring a drought is the first step of relief, not the last. Rs 8,500 per hectare barely covers the cost of one season, and sharecroppers and farmers without leases are often left out of the count. The real test will be how quickly the money and work arrive, and in whose hands.

When nearly half the country's land is in drought, this is no longer the story of one bad year of weather. Lasting arrangements for saving water, for fodder and for herders must now be part of every year's policy, not of an emergency package.
sawal: When will drought compensation reach the sharecropper?
ref: Drought Manual 2016
The central government's Manual for Drought Management, which tells states how to declare drought on measures of rainfall, crops, soil moisture and water.
India Drought Monitor
IIT Gandhinagar's drought tracking system, which uses satellite and weather data to map the current state of drought across the country.

h: The Adivasis of Andaman and Nicobar need self-rule, not handouts
dek: Researcher Manish Chandi, who has worked for decades with the islands' indigenous communities, says illegal fishing, big projects and misguided welfare schemes are taking away their self-reliance.
body: The indigenous communities of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, whether those who keep away from the outside world or those who have come into contact, are under pressure from many sides today. This Mongabay report rests on a conversation with researcher Manish Chandi, who has worked for decades among these communities with the Andaman Nicobar Environment Team and the Nature Conservation Foundation.

According to Chandi, the tribal reserves of communities like the Sentinelese of North Sentinel and the Shompen of Great Nicobar are the islands' richest places for biodiversity, richer even than the roughly 100 government national parks and sanctuaries there. The reason is that these areas are large, and they have seen neither logging nor settlers coming in from outside.

The threats are clear. Commercial trawlers and poachers enter the coastal buffer zones and carry off sharks, lobsters and turtles on which these communities depend to live. In Great Nicobar, the government's proposed development project falls on the Shompen's ancestral lands and settlements, and has been brought in without their consent.

Chandi also points to a less visible danger. He says some officials see hunting and gathering as backwardness and replace the food the communities grow or gather themselves with rations from outside. This increases dependence on the market, squeezes people into small settled villages, and opens the way to removing protected status from their large traditional territories and opening them up to tourism.

In his view, self-rule and self-reliance are the true measure of these communities' well-being, so welfare schemes should be shaped by their own outlook. He also says the administration has long shied away from understanding these communities in an ethical and scientific way and sharing that understanding with the people settled on the islands.
nazar: Separating Adivasis from their land and way of life in the name of development and welfare is no new story in India, from Bastar to Niyamgiri. The difference in the Andamans is that some communities are so small that one wrong decision can become a question of their survival.
The debate on the Great Nicobar project often shrinks to trees and coral reefs. Chandi's words remind us that the biggest question is consent: were the people whose land it is asked or not?
sawal: Development for whom, if those it affects were never asked?
ref: Shompen
A hunter-gatherer community living in the dense forests of Great Nicobar island, regarded as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, which mostly stays away from outside contact.
Great Nicobar project
The central government's large plan to build a port, an airport, a power plant and a new town in the island's south, which has drawn questions over forest felling and Adivasi rights.

h: A poet of Gaza: in war, to write is to bear witness
dek: Samalochan has published five poems by Palestinian poet Nasser Rabah in Anup Sethi's Hindi translation, along with the poet's own statement.
body: Five poems by Gaza poet Nasser Rabah have appeared in Hindi on Samalochan. Anup Sethi translated them from English, and the English versions were made from the Arabic original by other translators. So before reaching the reader, these poems have already travelled through two languages.

The first poem mourns friends who were killed. Candles burn at night, and small everyday things, a vegetable basket, a bus ticket, a recipe, are set beside the metallic taste of bullets. In the end all that is left is the distance between the flower seller and the graveyard, as if the war has swallowed everything else.

The second poem is a list of ordinary tasks the war has made impossible: playing music, tending a garden, painting doors. Neighbours arrive with chairs and condolences, salt is scattered on the threshold, and the house is empty of birds and mothers. In the third poem the poet walks around with emptiness in his pocket and finally begins a tired, gentle conversation with that same emptiness. In the fourth, clothes that have been taken off wander the cold rooms at night as ghosts, and the fifth, a long poem in three parts, turns songs into gravestones and speaks of the loss of a homeland through sunken ships, anchors and a stopped clock.

Before the poems comes Rabah's statement. For him writing is an endless struggle like the stone of Sisyphus, through which he proves that he exists. In days of war he writes less to make poetry than to bear witness, so that conscience survives. He describes Gaza as a place made of many communities and full of contradictions.
Rabah was born in 1963, studied agricultural science, and has written six poetry collections and two novels; his work has been translated into English, French and Hebrew.
nazar: There is plenty of news about Gaza in Hindi, but little of Gaza's own voice. These poems do not count the dead; they show the house where no one is left to paint the door. If this pain still arrives after passing through two translations, that is a victory for translation too.
sawal: When the home itself is gone, for whom should the poem be written?
ref: Nasser Rabah
A Palestinian poet and novelist living in Gaza, born 1963. His poems written amid the war have been translated into several languages.
Sisyphus
A figure from Greek myth punished to push a stone up a mountain, only for it to roll down every time. A metaphor for endless, fruitless labour.
photo_note: Shiva mourning Sati, a Kalighat pat painting

h: Childhood memories of Nainital: where the son was the heir and the daughters were questions
dek: The third part of Mrinal Pande's memoir series brings Shivani's night-time writing, the history of her mother's family and a girl's first questions.
body: The third part of senior writer and journalist Mrinal Pande's memoir series 'Bhakhai Akath Katha Birtant' (telling the untold story) has appeared on Jankipul. This time the story is in Nainital, where, after the father's many transfers, the family has settled into a large, leafy government house. A younger brother has been born, and the household feels the family is now complete.

At the centre of this part is her mother, Gaura Pant, whom Hindi readers know as Shivani. All day she combed her three daughters' hair, checked homework and Sanskrit lessons and fed her little son, and at night, after everyone was asleep, she wrote stories and novels on loose sheets at the dining table. The writer says few people at home valued this labour.

When the brother was born, an uncle called him the heir of the family, and it settled in the little girl's mind that girls were not wanted as much. On the day of Kanya Puja (the worship of young girls) she asked why, if grown-ups worship goddesses, they do not care about girls. In reply she was branded proud and stubborn, and she learnt to keep quiet.

This part also opens up her mother's family and her father's past: the death of her father's first wife from tuberculosis, then his second marriage to Gaura, who had studied at Santiniketan, and the history of the Almora family that served as diwans in princely states and whose name is linked, through Madan Mohan Malaviya, with Banaras Hindu University.

Around this time the writer's first poem was published in the children's magazine 'Parag', and a money order of ten rupees arrived, with which she bought her first book. The part ends as school reopens, with a return to the place where the girl felt safe.
nazar: This memoir shows that the work of a major Hindi writer was made between the kitchen and the children, in hours stolen from the night. The girl's question about the difference between son and daughter is as fresh today, because the answer is still so often the same silence.
sawal: How many mothers' writing never left the table at night?
ref: Shivani
Gaura Pant (1923-2003), a popular Hindi fiction writer, known for her novels about life in Kumaon. Mrinal Pande is her daughter.
Parag
A well-known Hindi monthly magazine for children, published by the Times group, in which many writers saw their first work in print.

h: Márquez in Galicia: rain, a grandmother and the memory of food
dek: Gabriel García Márquez's 1983 memoir essay in Manoj Mohan's Hindi translation, in which a journey leads back to a childhood kitchen.
by: Gabriel García Márquez (translated by Manoj Mohan)
body: Jankipul has published in Hindi a short memoir essay by Gabriel García Márquez, 'Galicia mein dharasar barish' (Pouring rain in Galicia). The original is from 1983, and the translation is by poet and writer Manoj Mohan. The introduction reminds us that Márquez is loved not only for his novels but just as much for his prose and memoirs.

The essay begins in Madrid, where Márquez, surrounded by photographers and journalists, is quietly told by an old friend, the painter and poet Héctor Rojas Herazo, that he should sometimes give himself a gift too. Márquez realises that for years he has done nothing for himself, and he fulfils an old dream of going to Galicia, in Spain's northwest.

The heart of the essay is his grandmother. In the big house at Aracataca she baked bread, and when a flood broke the oven she began drying pork to make ham. As a child he disliked the taste, but years later in Barcelona a single slice brought all the memories back. In Galicia Márquez begins to understand his grandmother's hospitality and her quirks, and a friend jokes that she must have been Galician.

The city of Santiago de Compostela wins him over at first sight, with plants growing out of its walls and its carved stone. He also muses, laughing, on the difference between a tourist and a traveller. It rains out of season for three days and his hosts keep apologising, but Márquez feels that Galicia without rain would be dull, a land whose poets have written about rain and wind for centuries.
In the end he asks himself whether his memories of Galicia are real, or whether, like his grandmother, he too has fallen under some spell.
nazar: Behind Márquez's great novels lies this same fine eye that can read a whole childhood in the taste of one food. For the Hindi reader, this essay is a reminder that travel writing can be a journey within as much as a journey to a place.
sawal: Which taste takes you back to your childhood home?
ref: Galicia
A region in Spain's northwest, known for its rain, its seafood and a language of its own. Santiago de Compostela is its historic pilgrim city.
Aracataca
The town in Colombia where Márquez spent his childhood in his grandparents' house. It is seen as the inspiration for his imaginary town of Macondo.

h: Leonia: a city made new every day, buried under its own rubbish
dek: With the fifteenth part of its translation of Calvino's 'Invisible Cities', Sammukh begins a new series called 'Changing Cities'.
body: On Sammukh, young fiction writer Suman Shekhar is publishing his Hindi translation of Italo Calvino's book 'Invisible Cities' in parts, under the title 'Adrishya Shahar'. The fifteenth part begins a new series within the book, 'Changing Cities', and its first city is Leonia.

Leonia remakes itself every morning. People wake in new sheets, bathe with new soap, put on new clothes and take packaged food out of new fridges. Yesterday's life waits outside in transparent bags for the rubbish truck: empty tubes, burnt-out bulbs, old newspapers, even pianos and whole sets of dishes. Calvino's narrator says the city's wealth lies less in what it makes than in what it throws away.

The street cleaners are welcomed almost like angels, but no one asks where the rubbish goes. Today's rubbish neither rots nor burns, so mountains of it keep rising around the city. It is the same with neighbouring cities; their borders have become walls of debris, and there is a fear that one day it will all collapse and bury Leonia in its own past.

In the second half of the part, Kublai Khan and Marco Polo sit on swings in a garden and argue. Polo suggests that the workers of ports and mines, washerwomen, cooks and rubbish collectors perhaps exist only as long as someone thinks of them. Kublai admits he never thinks of them, yet without them this comfort would not be possible. The conversation ends on the riddle of who really exists, those who labour or those who rest.
nazar: This fifty-year-old text reads like a direct comment on our city life today: rubbish mountains like Delhi's Ghazipur, and the people who haul the waste and whom no one thinks about. Translations like this give our own debates a new language in Hindi.
sawal: On whose life does the rubbish we throw away finally fall?
ref: Italo Calvino
Italian writer (1923-1985). In 'Invisible Cities' (1972), Marco Polo describes imaginary cities to Kublai Khan.
Kublai Khan
Thirteenth-century Mongol emperor, grandson of Genghis Khan. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo spent years at his court.
photo_note: Temples and ghats of Banaras, Edwin Lord Weeks

h: Kolkata's Nobels and the translation crisis of Bangla
dek: This instalment of Baby Shaw's column 'C/O Bengal' counts how many Nobels Bengal has seen, how many it missed, and why Bangla literature has reached the world so little.
body: On Hindwi's blog 'Bela', a new instalment of Baby Shaw's column 'C/O Bengal' explores the relationship between the Nobel Prize and Bengal. The writer argues that Bengal's tradition of knowledge is far larger than the Nobel list, but Bangla literature's recognition in the world has stayed tied down by the lack of translation.

It begins with six winners who had some link with Kolkata: Ronald Ross (1902, research on malaria), Rabindranath Tagore (1913, literature), C.V. Raman (1930, physics), Mother Teresa (1979, peace), Amartya Sen (1998) and Abhijit Banerjee (2019, economics). The writer makes clear that not all of them were Bengali, but Kolkata is a common thread in their stories: some did research here, some studied, some served.

Then come the names that reached nomination but not the prize. Satyendra Nath Bose, after whom the boson particle is named, was nominated several times. Meghnad Saha's name appears in physics nominations for more than two decades, as does that of Upendranath Brahmachari, who made a drug for kala-azar. In literature, Tarashankar Bandyopadhyay's name is found in the records for 1971, the year he died. The writer warns against reading too much into such records.

The article's real concern is translation. Mentioning prose writers such as Bibhutibhushan, Manik Bandyopadhyay, Mahasweta Devi and Advaita Mallabarman, and poets such as Jibanananda Das, Shankha Ghosh and Joy Goswami, she says there is no shortage of talent; what is missing is a plan to carry it into the world's languages.

She proposes a well-thought-out translation movement: training for translators, fair pay, and the support of academies and publishers. And she reminds us that the Nobel is an honour, not a destination.
nazar: This is not about Bangla alone, but about Hindi, Urdu and every Indian language. A good translator gets neither money nor recognition, and then we wonder why the world does not know our books. Translation between Indian languages matters just as much as translation into English.
sawal: Do we give our translators their due?
ref: Satyendra Nath Bose
Kolkata physicist (1894-1974). With Einstein he laid the foundation of Bose-Einstein statistics, and 'bosons' are named after him.
Advaita Mallabarman
Bangla novelist (1914-1951), known for 'Titash Ekti Nadir Naam' (A river called Titash), his novel about a fishing community.

h: Everest's Green Boots: a body under the wrong name for thirty years
dek: Hari Karki retells the story of the 1996 ITBP expedition, one of whose members' bodies served for three decades as a marker on the climbing route.
body: This instalment of Hari Karki's column 'Gham-Pani' (sun and rain) on Hindwi's 'Bela' is the story of Everest's most famous body. In cities a landmark is an old banyan tree or a bridge, but in the 'death zone' above eight thousand metres the dead themselves become landmarks. On the climbing route from the Tibetan side, at about 8,500 metres, lies a body in green boots that climbers have long called 'Green Boots'.

For thirty years it was believed to be ITBP Head Constable Tsewang Paljor. According to the writer, a DNA test in 2026 showed that the body is that of his comrade, Lance Naik Dorje Morup, and there are now plans to bring it down.

The writer then retraces the 1996 expedition day by day. Led by Commandant Mohinder Singh, the team wanted to be the first Indian team to climb Everest by the northern route. On 10 May the summit party set out late, the ropes ran short, and three men, Paljor, Morup and the experienced Tsewang Smanla, kept going. In the evening the radio brought news that they had reached the summit, but those watching from below reckoned they were well short of it. That same evening a blizzard struck and the three did not return.

The article also questions the conduct of a Japanese team that passed these injured climbers on the way up and did not stop. The writer says books and blogs repeated the Paljor identification again and again, though some old documents had named the body as Morup.
In the end the question arises of how dangerous it is to bring down a frozen body from such a height, and why the Sherpas, who regard Chomolungma as a mother, are against disturbing the dead.
nazar: This article shows the cold truth behind the romantic picture of Everest: soldiers of a government expedition whose very names were written wrongly for thirty years. When does a human being become a landmark in the race to conquer a mountain? For the Sherpas and labourers of the Himalayan regions, that question is even bigger.
sawal: Whom do the dead left on the mountain belong to, their families or the mountain?
ref: ITBP
The Indo-Tibetan Border Police, the central armed force that guards the Himalayan border. It has a long history in mountaineering.
Death zone
Altitudes above eight thousand metres, where oxygen is so thin that the body cannot survive for long.
